lesson.title: The Extrema Hiding at the Edges
lesson.summary: On a closed or restricted domain, the highest and lowest points of a function can sit right at the boundary rather than at a critical point, and finding them takes a different check than the usual derivative test.
lesson.body:
The Closed Interval Method tells you that a continuous function on a closed interval [a, b] is guaranteed to attain both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum somewhere on that interval. The candidates for those extreme values are the critical points inside the interval (where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) is undefined) and the two endpoints, x = a and x = b. Endpoint extrema are the values that turn up at those boundary points, and they deserve their own name because they behave differently from local extrema.

A local extremum, found by the First Derivative Test, requires a full two sided neighborhood: the function has to be doing one thing just to the left of the point and the opposite thing just to the right. An endpoint only has one side available, since the domain simply stops there. That means an endpoint can be an extreme value of the function on its restricted domain even when the derivative is not zero there, and even when there is no sign change to check on both sides, because there is no "both sides" to check.

Here is how to classify what is happening at an endpoint: evaluate the function there, then look at the one sided behavior of f' moving from the endpoint into the interior of the domain. If f is decreasing as you move away from a left endpoint, that endpoint is the top of a local slide down, an endpoint local maximum. If f is increasing as you move away from a left endpoint, it is an endpoint local minimum. The logic mirrors at a right endpoint: if f is increasing as you approach it, the curve is climbing right up to the boundary, so it is an endpoint local maximum; if f is decreasing as you approach it, it is an endpoint local minimum.

Consider f(x) = x^3 - 3x on the closed interval [0, 3]. First find the critical points: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x - 1)(x + 1), so f'(x) = 0 at x = -1 and x = 1. Only x = 1 lies inside [0, 3], so it is the only interior critical point to check. Now evaluate f at that critical point and at both endpoints: f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1 - 3 = -2, and f(3) = 27 - 9 = 18. Comparing these three candidate values, the absolute maximum on [0, 3] is 18, attained at the right endpoint x = 3, and the absolute minimum is -2, attained at the interior critical point x = 1.

Notice what makes x = 0 and x = 3 endpoint extrema rather than critical-point extrema: f'(0) = 3(0) - 3 = -3 and f'(3) = 3(9) - 3 = 24, and neither of those is zero. These points never would have shown up from solving f'(x) = 0. At x = 0, f is decreasing as it leaves the endpoint (f'(0) < 0), so x = 0 is an endpoint local maximum on its restricted domain, even though it is not the global maximum (0 < 18). At x = 3, f is increasing as it approaches (f'(3) > 0), so x = 3 is an endpoint local maximum too, and since 18 is larger than every other candidate, it is also the absolute maximum. The interior point x = 1 is a genuine local minimum in the ordinary sense, confirmed by the sign change of f' from negative to positive there.

It is worth seeing what happens if the domain is opened up instead. On the open interval (0, 3), the endpoints are excluded entirely, so neither x = 0 nor x = 3 can be an extremum of any kind. In fact, the function would have no absolute maximum at all on (0, 3): as x approaches 3 from the left, f(x) approaches 18 but never actually reaches it, since x = 3 is not in the domain. This is exactly why the Closed Interval Method requires a closed, bounded interval. Take away the closure, and the guarantee of an attained maximum and minimum disappears along with the endpoints that would have produced them.
